title: Our Island Story
sourceTitle: Our Island Story: A Child's History of England (US edition: An Island Story: A History of England for Boys and Girls, 1920)
author: H. E. Marshall
licenseEvidence: First published London 1905 (T. C. & E. C. Jack); this US edition published New York 1920 (Frederick A. Stokes) — both before 1930, so public domain in the USA. Author H. E. Marshall died 1941, so also public domain in life+70 countries. Online text: A Celebration of Women Writers (UPenn), transcribed by Ambleside Online volunteers. Not available on Project Gutenberg.
description: The beloved classic read-aloud history of Britain, told as a chain of stories from the legends of Albion to the early twentieth century. Siblings listen together, narrate the chapter back, find the place on a map, and add a date to the family timeline. The full text of this classic is free online.
includes: 114 lessons in 13 units, one chapter each
Link to the free full text for every chapter
Narration, map work, and timeline steps for each lesson
Questions with answers for every chapter
Parent notes where legend mixes with history or the book shows its imperial-era viewpoint

units.title: Unit 1: Ancient Britain and the Romans (Chapters 1–8)

lessons.title: Chapter 1: The Stories of Albion and Brutus
steps: Read chapter 1 aloud together
Narrate how the little mermaid won Albion his island and how Brutus came to rename it
Find Great Britain on a world map, then point to the white cliffs of Dover on its south coast
Add 'Albion and Brutus (legend)' to the legends strip at the start of your timeline
questions: Who was Albion's father, and what did he rule?
What was the island called before Albion took it over?
Where did Brutus sail from, and what name did he give the islands?
answers: Neptune, king of the sea and the waves
Samothea
From Troy; he called them Britain (Britannia), after himself
lessons.notes: This chapter is myth and legend, not history; the book itself says it may be only a fairy tale. The closing lines about 'Greater Britain' reflect the book's 1900s imperial outlook and could prompt a short talk.

lessons.title: Chapter 2: The Coming of the Romans
steps: Read chapter 2 aloud together
Narrate how the Roman standard-bearer leaped into the sea and how the British war chariots fought
Find the Strait of Dover between France and Kent on a map, where Caesar crossed
Add 'Julius Caesar's first landing in Britain, 55 BC' to your timeline
questions: Why did Julius Caesar want to conquer Britain?
What did the Romans carry instead of a flag?
What stuck out from the wheels of the British war chariots?
answers: He heard it was rich in tin, lead and other metals, with pearls on its shores
A golden eagle on a pole
Swords

lessons.title: Chapter 3: The Romans Come Again
steps: Read chapter 3 aloud together
Narrate how Cassivellaunus led the Britons and how Caesar finally left the island
Locate the Thames valley north of London on a map of England, where Cassivellaunus led the Britons
Add 'Caesar's second invasion, 54 BC' to your timeline
questions: How many ships did Caesar bring the second time?
Why were British swords weaker than Roman ones?
What do the letters B.C. and A.D. mean?
answers: About eight hundred
They were made of soft copper, which bent easily
B.C. means before Christ; A.D. (Anno Domini) means in the year of our Lord

lessons.title: Chapter 4: How Caligula Conquered Britain, and How Caractacus Refused to Be Conquered
steps: Read chapter 4 aloud together
Narrate Caligula's seashell 'conquest' and what Caractacus said to the Emperor Claudius
Find the Welsh borders near Shropshire on a map, where Caractacus made his last stand
Add 'Claudius invades Britain, AD 43' and 'Caractacus captured, AD 51' to your timeline
questions: What did Caligula order his soldiers to gather on the beach?
What was a Roman Triumph?
What did Claudius do after hearing Caractacus speak?
answers: Seashells
A victory parade through Rome with the conqueror, his soldiers, and his captives
He set Caractacus and his family free
lessons.notes: Caligula's seashell episode comes from Roman writers and may be exaggerated. The site of Caractacus's last battle is not known for certain.

lessons.title: Chapter 5: The Story of a Warrior Queen
steps: Read chapter 5 aloud together
Narrate why Boadicea rose against the Romans and what she said to her people
Find Norfolk and Suffolk, then London and St Albans, on a map of England
Add 'Boadicea (Boudica) leads the revolt, AD 60–61' to your timeline
questions: Which part of Britain did Boadicea rule?
What did her husband do with his wealth before he died?
What was St Albans called in Roman times?
answers: The land now called Norfolk and Suffolk
He gave half to the Emperor and half to his wife and daughters
Verulamium
lessons.notes: This chapter describes the sacking of towns and ends with Boadicea poisoning herself and her daughters; parents may want to preview it for younger children.

lessons.title: Chapter 6: The Last of the Romans
steps: Read chapter 6 aloud together
Narrate the good things Agricola did in Britain and why Hadrian built his wall
Trace Hadrian's Wall from the Tyne to the Solway on a map of northern England
Add 'Hadrian's Wall begun, AD 122' and 'Romans leave Britain, c. 410' to your timeline
questions: Name two good things Agricola did for the Britons.
Who were the British priests, and which tree did they hold sacred?
About what year did the Romans leave Britain?
answers: He lowered taxes, built schools and courts, and taught people to read and write
The Druids; the oak tree
About AD 410
lessons.notes: The book's picture of the ancient Britons as 'ignorant and wild' reflects its era; archaeology shows a skilled Iron Age culture. Worth a brief talk.

lessons.title: Chapter 7: The Story of St. Alban
steps: Read chapter 7 aloud together
Narrate how Alban hid Amphibalus and took his place before the governor
Find St Albans, north of London, on a map of England
Add 'Martyrdom of St Alban, c. 304' to your timeline (the exact date is uncertain)
questions: Why did Amphibalus come to Alban's house?
How did Alban trick the soldiers?
What is the hill where Alban died called today?
answers: He was a Christian fleeing the Emperor's soldiers and needed a hiding place
He put on Amphibalus's robe and hood so they took him for the priest
Holywell Hill
lessons.notes: Alban's execution by beheading is told plainly. The book itself says the miracles at his death need not be believed.

lessons.title: Chapter 8: Vortigern and King Constans
steps: Read chapter 8 aloud together
Narrate how Vortigern made Constans king and then plotted to take the power himself
Find Hadrian's Wall, then Brittany in north-west France, on a map
Add 'The Groans of the Britons appeal to Rome, c. 446' to your timeline
questions: What was the Britons' sad letter to Rome called?
What was Constans before he became king?
Where did Aurelius Ambrosius and Uther Pendragon flee?
answers: The Groans of the Britons
A monk
To Brittany in France
lessons.notes: Constans, Vortigern's plot, and Uther Pendragon come from Geoffrey of Monmouth's legendary history; the 'Groans' letter is from the early writer Gildas. The murder of Constans is told plainly.

lessons.title: Chapter 9: The Story of the Coming of Hengist and Horsa
steps: Read chapter 9 aloud together
Narrate how Hengist won land with an ox-hide thong and how Rowena met Vortigern
Find Kent, then Caistor near Lincoln, on a map of England
Add 'Hengist and Horsa land in Kent, 449' to your timeline
questions: Why did Vortigern invite the Saxons to Britain?
How did Hengist make one leather thong surround so much land?
What did Hengist get in return for letting Vortigern marry Rowena?
answers: To help fight the Picts and Scots
He cut a bullock's hide round and round into one long thin strip
The whole of Kent
lessons.notes: Hengist, Horsa and the date 449 come from early chronicles; the thong trick and Rowena are legend. Try the paper-spiral experiment the book suggests.

lessons.title: Chapter 10: Hengist's Treachery
steps: Read chapter 10 aloud together
Narrate what happened at the May feast on Salisbury Plain and how Vortigern met his end
Find Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, then Wales, on a map
Add 'The treachery of the long knives (legend), 5th century' to your timeline
questions: Where did Hengist's men hide their daggers?
How did Edol, Earl of Gloucester, escape?
How did Aurelius and Uther capture Vortigern's castle?
answers: In their stockings
He fought with a wooden stake he found on the ground
They piled wood around it and set it on fire
lessons.notes: This chapter is legend from Geoffrey of Monmouth and includes a massacre and Vortigern burning in his castle; consider previewing for young listeners.

lessons.title: Chapter 11: The Story of How the Giant's Dance Was Brought to Britain
steps: Read chapter 11 aloud together
Narrate how Merlin brought the Giant's Dance from Ireland and where the stones were set up
Find Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire on a map of England
Put 'Merlin and the Giant's Dance (legend)' on your legends strip; Stonehenge itself was built c. 3000–2000 BC
questions: Who cut off Hengist's head?
Where did Merlin say the Giant's Dance stood?
What did Aurelius rename the Giant's Dance?
answers: Edol, Earl of Gloucester
In Ireland
Stonehenge
lessons.notes: The book admits this is probably a fairy tale. Stonehenge is real but was built thousands of years before Merlin's supposed time; a picture of it makes a good discussion starter.

lessons.title: Chapter 12: The Coming of Arthur
steps: Read chapter 12 aloud together
Narrate how Merlin brought Arthur to the nobles and what happened with the sword in the stone
Find Cornwall and Wales, the lands tied to the Arthur stories, on a map of Britain
Add 'King Arthur (legend), c. 500' to your legends strip
questions: Whose son did Merlin say Arthur was?
What was written beneath the sword in the stone?
What were the names of Arthur's sword and spear?
answers: Uther Pendragon's
Whoever could draw it out was the rightful king of Britain
Excalibur and Ron
lessons.notes: Arthur is a figure of legend; a British war leader may lie behind the stories, but nothing is certain. The verse is from Tennyson's 'Idylls of the King.'

lessons.title: Chapter 13: The Founding of the Round Table
steps: Read chapter 13 aloud together
Narrate the quarrel at the Easter feast and how a round table solved it
Find Winchester in Hampshire, where a medieval 'Round Table' hangs, on a map of England
Add 'Knights of the Round Table (legend)' to your legends strip
questions: What were the nobles fighting about at the Easter feast?
Why did a round table stop the quarreling?
What did Arthur teach about being brave?
answers: Who would get the best seats near the top of the table
It has no top or bottom, so every knight was equal
That you can be brave yet kind, and strong yet gentle
lessons.notes: Legend, not history. The Winchester Round Table was made around 1290, centuries after Arthur's supposed time.

lessons.title: Chapter 14: The Story of Gregory and the Pretty Children
steps: Read chapter 14 aloud together
Narrate what Gregory said about the children in the Roman market and how Augustine came to England
Find Rome in Italy, then Canterbury in Kent, on a map of Europe
Add 'Augustine arrives in Kent, 597' to your timeline
questions: What did Gregory say when he heard the children were Angles?
Which king first listened to Augustine?
What did the priest Coifi do to the old idol?
answers: Not Angles but angels
Ethelbert, King of Kent
He rode at it with a spear and knocked it over
lessons.notes: The children were being sold as slaves; a short talk about slavery may help. Coifi's story actually happened in Northumbria, not Kent.

lessons.title: Chapter 15: How King Alfred Learned to Read
steps: Read chapter 15 aloud together
Narrate how Alfred won his mother's book of songs
Find Wessex in southern England, and Wantage, Alfred's birthplace, on a map
Add 'Alfred born at Wantage, 849' to your timeline
questions: Where did the Danes come from?
What was Alfred's mother's name?
How did Alfred win the book?
answers: Denmark, Norway and Sweden
Osburga
He was the first of the brothers to learn to read it

lessons.title: Chapter 16: King Alfred in the Cowherd's Cottage
steps: Read chapter 16 aloud together
Narrate how Alfred burned the cakes and what the cowherd's wife said
Find the Somerset Levels (marshes) in south-west England on a map
Add 'Alfred hides in the Somerset marshes, 878' to your timeline
questions: Why did Alfred build ships?
What was the cowherd's name?
What was Alfred thinking about while the cakes burned?
answers: To stop the Danes at sea before they could land
Denewulf
His kingdom, and how to free his people from the Danes
lessons.notes: The cake story is a much later legend, not recorded in Alfred's lifetime. The poem quoted is Thomas Campbell's 'Ye Mariners of England.'

lessons.title: Chapter 17: More About Alfred the Great
steps: Read chapter 17 aloud together
Narrate how Alfred spied on the Danes as a minstrel and what he did once peace came
Find Athelney and Wedmore in Somerset on a map of England
Add 'Alfred defeats the Danes at Edington; Peace of Wedmore, 878' to your timeline
questions: What does Athelney mean?
What was the Danes' magic banner called?
How did Alfred keep track of the hours?
answers: The Isle of Nobles
The Raven
With marked candles that each burned for one hour
lessons.notes: The minstrel disguise is a later legend. Trial by jury grew up over centuries rather than being created by Alfred alone.

units.title: Unit 3: Danes, Saxons, and the Norman Conquest (Chapters 18–26)

lessons.title: Chapter 18: Ethelred the Unready
steps: Read chapter 18 aloud together
Narrate how Ethelred tried to buy off the Danes and what Danegelt was
Find Mercia in the English Midlands, then Denmark across the North Sea, on a map
Add 'St Brice's Day massacre of the Danes, 13 November 1002' to your timeline
questions: Who was the Lady of Mercia?
What did 'Unready' mean for Ethelred?
What was Danegelt?
answers: Ethelfleda, Alfred's daughter and Edward the Elder's sister
He was foolish and slow (it really meant 'badly advised')
A tax the people paid so the king could pay the Danes to go away
lessons.notes: The massacre of Danish families, including Gunhilda's death, is described in some detail; consider previewing. The book gives Alfred's death as 901, but it was 899.

lessons.title: Chapter 19: How Edmund Ironside Fought for the Crown
steps: Read chapter 19 aloud together
Narrate Edmund Ironside's single combat with Canute and how they agreed to share England
Find Normandy in northern France on a map, where Ethelred fled
Add 'Edmund Ironside and Canute divide England, 1016' to your timeline
questions: Why did Sweyn of Denmark attack England?
Why was Edmund called Ironside?
Which part of England did each king rule after the fight?
answers: To avenge the murder of his sister Gunhilda
Because of his strength and courage
Edmund ruled the south and Canute the north
lessons.notes: The single combat comes from later chroniclers and may not have happened. In 1016 Edmund actually kept Wessex while Canute took the rest.

lessons.title: Chapter 20: Canute and the Waves
steps: Read chapter 20 aloud together
Narrate how Canute answered his flattering nobles at the seashore
Find Winchester in Hampshire, and Denmark and Norway across the North Sea, on a map
Add 'Canute becomes king of all England, 1016' and 'Canute dies, 1035' to your timeline
questions: Besides England, which countries did Canute rule?
What lesson did Canute teach by sitting before the waves?
Into how many earldoms did Canute divide England?
answers: Denmark, Norway and Sweden
That only God has power over the sea, not any king
Four
lessons.notes: The waves story was first written down about a century after Canute and is probably legend; note that Canute was showing the limits of a king's power, not trying to command the sea.

lessons.title: Chapter 21: Edward the Confessor
steps: Read chapter 21 aloud together
Narrate the fight at Dover and why Earl Godwin refused to punish the townspeople
Find Dover in Kent and Normandy across the Channel on a map
Add 'Edward the Confessor dies; Westminster Abbey consecrated, 1066' to your timeline
questions: Why did Edward the Confessor prefer the Normans?
What did Godwin say when Edward ordered him to punish Dover?
How did Harold end up in Duke William's power?
answers: He had grown up in Normandy
That the king had heard only one side of the story
His ship was wrecked on the coast of Normandy

lessons.title: Chapter 22: Harold
steps: Read chapter 22 aloud together
Narrate Harold's crowning and how Duke William took the news
Find Westminster in London and Rouen in Normandy on a map
Add 'Harold crowned king, January 1066' to your timeline
questions: Who was the real heir to the throne, and why wasn't he chosen?
What did Harold tell William's messenger about the crown?
What did William promise his nobles to get them to come?
answers: Edgar the Ætheling; he was a little boy raised in Hungary
That it was not his to give; the people had given it to him in trust
Land, castles and money taken from the English

lessons.title: Chapter 23: The Battle of Stamford Bridge
steps: Read chapter 23 aloud together
Narrate what Harold offered Tostig before the battle and what Tostig answered
Find York and Stamford Bridge in Yorkshire on a map of England
Add 'Battle of Stamford Bridge, 25 September 1066' to your timeline
questions: Who invaded the north with Tostig?
How much English land did Harold say Harold Hardrada would get?
Why had Harold's army gone home before this news came?
answers: Harold Hardrada, King of Norway
Seven feet for a grave, or a little more since he was so tall
It was autumn and they went home to bring in the harvest

lessons.title: Chapter 24: The Battle of Hastings
steps: Read chapter 24 aloud together
Narrate how William landed in England and how the battle on Senlac Hill was won and lost
Find Pevensey and Hastings on the Sussex coast, then the town of Battle, on a map
Add 'Battle of Hastings, 14 October 1066' to your timeline
questions: What did William say when he fell as he landed?
Why wouldn't Harold let Gurth burn the land between London and the coast?
Who rode out first for the Normans, singing?
answers: That he had already taken hold of his kingdom
He would never harm English homes or the people he was given to rule
Taillefer, a minstrel
lessons.notes: The battle was fought on 14 October 1066; the book's date of the 15th is a slip. The Bayeux Tapestry is a wonderful picture source to look at alongside.

lessons.title: Chapter 25: William the Conqueror – The Story of Hereward the Wake
steps: Read chapter 25 aloud together
Narrate how Hereward held out at Ely and how he was finally betrayed
Find Ely and the Fens in Cambridgeshire on a map of England
Add 'William crowned, Christmas 1066' and 'Hereward's stand at Ely, 1070–71' to your timeline
questions: Who would not crown William, and who crowned Harold?
How did William try to reach the camp at Ely?
Who betrayed Hereward, and why?
answers: Archbishop Stigand, who had also crowned Harold
He built a strong road across the marshes
The monks, who were tired of fighting and plain food
lessons.notes: Includes the Harrying of the North, a burned 'witch,' and mutilation of prisoners; preview for sensitive children. Stigand did not in fact crown Harold or William; the book follows older tradition.

lessons.title: Chapter 26: William the Conqueror – Death of the King
steps: Read chapter 26 aloud together
Narrate what the curfew and the Domesday Book were, and why William made them
Find the New Forest in Hampshire, then Caen in Normandy where William is buried, on a map
Add 'Domesday Book, 1086' and 'Death of William the Conqueror, 1087' to your timeline
questions: What does 'curfew' come from, and what did it mean?
What was written in the Domesday Book?
What did William destroy villages to make?
answers: French 'couvre feu,' meaning 'cover fire': put out lights and fires at eight
All the great houses and lands in the kingdom and who owned them
The New Forest, a hunting ground

units.title: Unit 4: Normans and the First Plantagenets (Chapters 27–36)

lessons.title: Chapter 27: The Story of William the Red
steps: Read chapter 27 aloud together
Narrate how William Rufus won English support and how he died in the forest
Find the New Forest in Hampshire and Winchester, where Rufus is buried, on a map
Add 'William Rufus killed in the New Forest, 1100' to your timeline
questions: Why was he called William Rufus?
What did Rufus promise the English to win their help?
Who was suspected of shooting the king?
answers: Because of his red hair
Lower taxes, more liberty, and protection from the Norman barons
Walter Tyrrell
lessons.notes: Whether Rufus's death was an accident or murder is still debated.

lessons.title: Chapter 28: Henry I. – The Story of the "White Ship"
steps: Read chapter 28 aloud together
Narrate the sinking of the White Ship and who survived to tell the story
Find Barfleur on the coast of Normandy and trace the crossing to England on a map
Add 'Wreck of the White Ship, 1120' to your timeline
questions: Why was Henry I called Beauclerc?
Why did Prince William turn the small boat back?
Who was the only survivor, and what may have helped save him?
answers: It means 'fine scholar'; he could read and write well
To save his sister Marie
Berthold, a butcher of Rouen; his warm sheepskin coat
lessons.notes: The shipwreck and drownings are told vividly and could upset a sensitive child.

lessons.title: Chapter 29: The Story of King Stephen
steps: Read chapter 29 aloud together
Narrate how Matilda escaped from Oxford over the snow and how Stephen and Henry made peace
Find Oxford and Wallingford on the River Thames, then Northallerton in Yorkshire, on a map
Add 'Matilda escapes Oxford, 1142' and 'Treaty of Wallingford, 1153' to your timeline
questions: Where does the name Plantagenet come from?
Why was it called the Battle of the Standard?
How did Matilda and her knights slip past Stephen's soldiers?
answers: From planta genista, the sprig of broom Geoffrey wore in his helmet
The English gathered round a pole on a cart hung with four saints' banners
They dressed in white and crossed the frozen Thames on the ice
lessons.notes: The cruelty in the barons' castles is mentioned briefly; this period is often called 'the Anarchy.'

lessons.title: Chapter 30: Henry Plantagenet – The Story of Gilbert and Rohesia
steps: Read chapter 30 aloud together
Narrate how Rohesia freed Gilbert and found him again in London
Find Jerusalem in the Holy Land, then London, on a map, and trace Rohesia's long journey
Add 'Henry II crowned, 1154' to your timeline (Gilbert and Rohesia are legend)
questions: What did Henry II make the barons do with their castles?
What were the only two English words Rohesia knew?
What was the name of Gilbert and Rohesia's son?
answers: Pull them down
Gilbert and London
Thomas (Thomas à Becket)
lessons.notes: The book says this tale may be only a fairy tale; Becket's mother was in fact a Norman woman. Its words for Muslims ('Mohametans,' 'Saracens') are dated.

lessons.title: Chapter 31: Henry Plantagenet – The Story of Thomas à Becket
steps: Read chapter 31 aloud together
Narrate how Henry and Becket went from close friends to bitter enemies
Find Canterbury in Kent on a map of England
Add 'Murder of Thomas Becket, 29 December 1170' to your timeline
questions: What happened with the beggar and Becket's cloak?
How did Becket change when he became archbishop?
What did Henry and Becket disagree about over priests who did wrong?
answers: The king pulled off Becket's fine cloak and gave it to the beggar
He gave up fine clothes, rich food and servants for a plain, hard life
Henry wanted them tried in the king's courts; Becket wanted bishops' courts
lessons.notes: Becket's killing in the cathedral is described step by step; preview for younger children.

lessons.title: Chapter 32: Henry Plantagenet – The Story of the Conquest of Ireland
steps: Read chapter 32 aloud together
Narrate how Henry showed sorrow for Becket's death and how Ireland came under the English king
Find Ireland, Dublin, and the four nations of the United Kingdom on a map
Add 'Henry II goes to Ireland, 1171–72' and 'Henry's penance at Canterbury, 1174' to your timeline
questions: How did Henry show he was sorry at Becket's grave?
Which Irish king asked Henry for help?
What news broke Henry's heart at the end of his life?
answers: He walked barefoot, prayed all night without food, and let monks beat his back
Dermot
That his favourite son John had rebelled against him too
lessons.notes: The book presents the Norman takeover of Ireland as a simple 'joining'; it was an invasion with a long, painful legacy, worth a short talk.

lessons.title: Chapter 33: The Story of Richard Cœur de Lion
steps: Read chapter 33 aloud together
Narrate why Richard went on crusade and how he was discovered in Austria
Find Palestine and Jerusalem, then Austria and Vienna, on a map; then Sherwood Forest near Nottingham
Add 'Richard I on the Third Crusade, 1190–92' and 'Richard captured in Austria, 1192' to your timeline
questions: What does 'crusade' mean, and where does the word come from?
What is a truce, and how long was Richard's truce with Saladin?
What gave away the page in the market?
answers: War of the cross, from the Latin crux
A promise not to fight for a set time; three years
He carried the king's rich embroidered gloves
lessons.notes: The book tells the Crusades only from the Christian side, and Robin Hood is legend. The page is beaten to make him talk.

lessons.title: Chapter 34: Richard Cœur de Lion – The Story of How Blondel Found the King
steps: Read chapter 34 aloud together
Narrate how Blondel found Richard and how the English got their king back
Find Germany and Trifels Castle, then Châlus in France where Richard died, on a map
Add 'Richard ransomed and freed, 1194' and 'Richard dies at Châlus, 1199' to your timeline
questions: How did Blondel know he had found the king?
What did the English have to pay to free Richard?
What did Richard do with the archer who shot him?
answers: Richard sang back the next part of their song from a window
A large ransom
He forgave him, set him free, and gave him a hundred shillings
lessons.notes: Blondel's search is a well-loved legend, not history. Richard hanging the castle's soldiers is mentioned briefly.

lessons.title: Chapter 35: John Lackland – The Story of Prince Arthur
steps: Read chapter 35 aloud together
Narrate how Arthur begged Hubert to spare his eyes
Find Brittany, then Rouen on the River Seine in Normandy, on a map
Add 'Prince Arthur disappears at Rouen, 1203' to your timeline
questions: Why was John called Lackland?
Who was the rightful heir to the throne?
What did Hubert do after Arthur pleaded with him?
answers: He was left no lands when his father died
Prince Arthur of Brittany, son of John's elder brother Geoffrey
He sent the men with the hot irons away
lessons.notes: Arthur's death is a dark story (the blinding threat comes from Shakespeare's 'King John'); how he really died is unknown. Preview for sensitive children.

lessons.title: Chapter 36: John Lackland – The Story of the Great Charter
steps: Read chapter 36 aloud together
Narrate how the barons made John seal the Great Charter and what it promised
Find Runnymede on the Thames near Windsor, then the Wash on the east coast, on a map
Add 'Magna Carta sealed at Runnymede, 15 June 1215' to your timeline
questions: What was an Interdict?
Who helped the barons write the Great Charter?
Name one promise in Magna Carta.
answers: A ban on all church services in the land
Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury
No free man may be imprisoned or ruined without a lawful judgment (or: justice will not be sold, denied, or delayed)
lessons.notes: The book spells it 'Langdon'; the usual spelling is Langton. Surviving copies are now in the British Library and some cathedrals.

units.title: Unit 5: Plantagenet Kings and the Hundred Years' War (Chapters 37–48)

lessons.title: Chapter 37: Henry III. of Winchester – The Story of Hubert de Burgh
steps: Read chapter 37 aloud together
Narrate how Hubert de Burgh beat the French fleet and how the smith refused to make his chains
Find Dover and Sandwich on the Kent coast, then the Tower of London, on a map
Add 'Hubert de Burgh defeats the French at sea, 1217' to your timeline
questions: How old was Henry III when he became king?
What trick did the English sailors use against the French?
What does 'taking sanctuary' mean?
answers: Nine
They threw quicklime into the wind so it blew into the Frenchmen's eyes
Fleeing to a church and holding the altar cross so no one dares harm you

lessons.title: Chapter 38: Henry III. of Winchester – The Story of Simon de Montfort
steps: Read chapter 38 aloud together
Narrate what Simon de Montfort did for the people and how his new council worked
Find Lewes in Sussex and Evesham in Worcestershire on a map of England
Add 'Battle of Lewes, 1264' and 'Simon de Montfort's Parliament, 1265' to your timeline
questions: What did Henry tell Simon he feared more than thunder?
What was special about the laws made at Oxford?
What does 'Parliament' mean?
answers: Simon himself
They were written in English
Talking-place
lessons.notes: The torture of a Jewish man for money is mentioned; the book calls Jews 'despised' without comment, which is worth discussing. Simon was killed at Evesham in 1265.

lessons.title: Chapter 39: Henry III. – The Story of the Poisoned Dagger
steps: Read chapter 39 aloud together
Narrate how the Emir's servant attacked Prince Edward and how Eleanor and the doctor helped him
Find Acre and Jaffa on a map of modern Israel
Add 'Prince Edward survives an assassin at Acre, 1272' to your timeline
questions: What did Princess Eleanor do as soon as she heard Edward was wounded?
Why did Edward call the servant who struck the dead slave a coward?
Why did Edward leave Palestine and sail for home?
answers: She sucked the poisoned wound.
Because the slave was already dead, so hitting him was neither brave nor honorable.
He heard his father, Henry III, was ill.
lessons.notes: The story of Eleanor sucking out the poison is a later legend; chroniclers of the time do not mention it. The attack scene is briefly violent.

lessons.title: Chapter 40: Edward I. – The Little War of Chalons
steps: Read chapter 40 aloud together
Narrate what a tournament was and how the Count of Chalons broke the rules
Find Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy on a map of France
Add 'The Little War of Chalons, 1273' to your timeline
questions: How many knights did the Count bring, and how many had been agreed?
Why would Edward not take the Count's sword himself?
What was given to the winner of a tournament?
answers: Two thousand, though one thousand had been agreed.
The Count had behaved unknightly, so Edward let a common soldier take it.
A crown of bay leaves.

lessons.title: Chapter 41: Edward I. – The Lawgiver – The Story of the First Prince of Wales
steps: Read chapter 41 aloud together
Narrate how Edward made money round and how Wales got a Prince who spoke no French or English
Find Caernarfon Castle and Mount Snowdon in North Wales on a map
Add 'Edward I conquers Wales; Llewellyn killed, 1282' and 'Edward of Caernarfon born, 1284' to your timeline
questions: Why did the people feel Edward I was truly an English king?
What did people do with coins before Edward made his new law?
Who was the prince Edward showed to the Welsh barons?
answers: He had an English name, was born and lived in England, spoke English, and loved his people.
They cut them into pieces to make change.
His baby son, born at Caernarvon Castle.
lessons.notes: The baby-prince story and Merlin's prophecy are legends; the real title 'Prince of Wales' was given to young Edward in 1301. Llewellyn's head being paraded on a spear is mentioned briefly.

lessons.title: Chapter 42: Edward I. – The Hammer of the Scots
steps: Read chapter 42 aloud together
Narrate how Edward came to choose John Balliol and what treasures he carried off from Scotland
Find Scone near Perth in Scotland and Westminster Abbey in London on a map
Add 'Edward I takes the Stone of Destiny to Westminster, 1296' and 'Edward I dies, 1307' to your timeline
questions: Who was the Maid of Norway, and what happened to her?
What was the Stone of Destiny said to be?
Name two of Edward I's nicknames.
answers: The little heir to Scotland's throne; she died on her way from Norway.
The stone Jacob used as a pillow when he dreamed of the ladder to heaven.
Any two of Longshanks, Hammer of the Scots, the Lawgiver, Edward of Westminster.
lessons.notes: The book says the Stone is still at Westminster; it was returned to Scotland in 1996 and is now shown in Perth, travelling to London only for coronations.

lessons.title: Chapter 43: Edward II. of Caernarvon – The Story of King Robert the Bruce and Bohun
steps: Read chapter 43 aloud together
Narrate how Bruce prepared the ground before battle and what happened when Bohun charged at him
Find Stirling Castle and the Bannock Burn in central Scotland on a map
Add 'Robert the Bruce slays Henry de Bohun, 23 June 1314' to your timeline
questions: How did Bruce make the firm ground dangerous for English horses?
What did Bruce mean when he told Randolph a rose had fallen from his crown?
What did Bruce say after defeating Bohun?
answers: He had pits dug, filled with gorse branches, and covered with turf.
Randolph had missed his chance to win honor by letting English horsemen slip past.
That he had broken his good ax.
lessons.notes: Bohun's death is described briefly but vividly (a split helmet). The chapter also tells of Piers Gaveston's killing.

lessons.title: Chapter 44: Edward II. of Caernarvon – The Story of the Battle of Bannockburn
steps: Read chapter 44 aloud together
Narrate how the camp followers helped win Bannockburn and how Edward II escaped
Find Stirling, the River Forth, Dunbar, and Berwick-upon-Tweed on a map
Add 'Battle of Bannockburn, 24 June 1314' to your timeline
questions: What did King Edward think the kneeling Scots were doing?
What was the 'new army' that frightened the English?
How did Edward II finally get back to England?
answers: Asking for mercy (but they were praying to God).
Servants and camp followers with cloths tied to poles for banners.
In a little fishing boat from Dunbar to Berwick.
lessons.notes: The chapter ends with Edward II being deposed and murdered in prison (1327); a parent may want to preview the last paragraph.

lessons.title: Chapter 45: Edward III. of Windsor – The Story of the Battle of Sluys
steps: Read chapter 45 aloud together
Narrate why the Hundred Years' War began and how the English won at Sluys
Find Sluis (Sluys) in the Netherlands, Ghent in Belgium, and Southampton in England on a map
Add 'English victory at sea at Sluys, 1340; Hundred Years' War begins' to your timeline
questions: Why did Edward III say he should be King of France?
What was the Christopher?
Who finally told King Philip about the defeat, and how?
answers: Because his mother Isabella was sister to the French king who died without a son.
An English ship the French had captured, which the English won back.
His court fool, with a joke that the English were too cowardly to jump into the sea.

lessons.title: Chapter 46: Edward III. of Windsor – The Story of the Battle of Crecy
steps: Read chapter 46 aloud together
Narrate how the English archers won at Crécy and why the King let his son 'win his spurs'
Find Crécy-en-Ponthieu in northern France on a map
Add 'Battle of Crécy, 26 August 1346' to your timeline
questions: Where did Edward III watch the battle from?
What does 'Ich dien' mean, and whose motto was it first?
What did Edward say when he picked up the lady's garter?
answers: A windmill.
'I serve'; the blind King of Bohemia's.
'Evil be to him who evil thinks' (Honi soit qui mal y pense).
lessons.notes: The Order of the Garter was founded around 1348; the dropped-garter tale and the Bohemian origin of the Prince of Wales feathers are traditions rather than proven history.

lessons.title: Chapter 47: Edward III. of Windsor – The Story of the Siege of Calais
steps: Read chapter 47 aloud together
Narrate how the six burghers offered themselves and how Queen Philippa saved them
Find Calais on the French coast across the Strait of Dover
Add 'Siege of Calais ends; the six burghers spared, 1347' to your timeline
questions: What did Edward do for the poor and old people sent out of Calais?
Who was the first man to offer himself?
How did the six men have to be dressed?
answers: Gave them a dinner and money and let them pass safely.
Eustace de St. Pierre.
In their shirts, bare-headed and barefoot, with ropes round their necks, carrying the keys.

lessons.title: Chapter 48: Edward III. of Windsor – The Story of the Battle of Poitiers
steps: Read chapter 48 aloud together
Narrate how the Black Prince won at Poitiers and how he treated King John afterward
Find Poitiers in France and Canterbury Cathedral in Kent on a map
Add 'Battle of Poitiers, 1356' and 'Black Death reaches England, 1348' to your timeline
questions: Who was taken prisoner at Poitiers?
What did the Black Prince do at supper that surprised King John?
What still hangs over the Black Prince's tomb?
answers: King John of France and his son.
He waited on him at table instead of sitting down.
His black armor.
lessons.notes: The Black Death is mentioned briefly; it killed perhaps a third or more of England's people.

units.title: Unit 6: Lancaster, York, and the Wars of the Roses (Chapters 49–59)

lessons.title: Chapter 49: Richard II. of Bordeaux – The Story of Wat Tyler's Rebellion
steps: Read chapter 49 aloud together
Narrate what started Wat Tyler's rebellion and what Richard did at Mile End and Smithfield
Find Blackheath, Mile End, Smithfield, and the Tower on a map of London
Add 'Peasants' Revolt led by Wat Tyler, 1381' to your timeline
questions: What was the poll-tax?
What did the people at Mile End ask the King for?
Who struck down Wat Tyler at Smithfield?
answers: A tax on every person over fourteen ('poll' means head).
To make them and their children free forever.
The Mayor of London.
lessons.notes: The book calls the peasants 'slaves'; historians say serfs or villeins, who were bound to the land. Includes riots, burnings, and executions.

lessons.title: Chapter 50: How King Richard II. Lost His Throne
steps: Read chapter 50 aloud together
Narrate how Henry of Bolingbroke came back to England and took Richard's crown
Find Flint Castle in North Wales and Pontefract in Yorkshire on a map
Add 'Richard II deposed; Henry IV becomes king, 1399' to your timeline
questions: What did Richard take that made Henry come back from exile?
Where did Richard and Henry meet?
Which of Richard's companions left him for Henry?
answers: The lands and money of Henry's father, John of Gaunt.
Flint Castle in Wales.
His favorite dog.

lessons.title: Chapter 51: Henry IV. of Bolingbroke – The Story of the Battle of Shrewsbury
steps: Read chapter 51 aloud together
Narrate why the Percies turned against Henry IV and what happened at Shrewsbury
Find Shrewsbury in Shropshire near the Welsh border on a map
Add 'Battle of Shrewsbury; Hotspur killed, 1403' to your timeline
questions: Why was Harry Percy called Hotspur?
Why did several knights dress like the King at Shrewsbury?
How did young Prince James of Scotland become Henry's prisoner?
answers: Because he was so quick and brave in battle.
Rebels had sworn to kill the King, so the knights acted as decoys.
His ship to France was captured by the English.

lessons.title: Chapter 52: Henry IV. of Bolingbroke – The Story of How Prince Hal Was Sent to Prison
steps: Read chapter 52 aloud together
Narrate how Judge Gascoigne sent Prince Hal to prison and what the King said about it
Find Monmouth in Wales, Hal's birthplace, and Westminster in London on a map
Add 'Henry IV dies; Prince Hal becomes Henry V, 1413' to your timeline
questions: What did Prince Hal do in the courtroom?
Why was the King pleased when he heard the story?
What did Hal take from his sleeping father's bedside?
answers: He struck the judge in the face.
He had a judge who dared do justice and a son who obeyed the law.
The crown.
lessons.notes: Both stories are traditional tales, made famous by Shakespeare (the verses are from Henry IV, Part 2), and are not proven history.

lessons.title: Chapter 53: Henry V. of Monmouth – The Story of the Battle of Agincourt
steps: Read chapter 53 aloud together
Narrate the tennis-ball insult and how the tired English army won at Agincourt
Find Harfleur, Azincourt (Agincourt), and Calais in northern France on a map
Add 'Battle of Agincourt, 25 October 1415' to your timeline
questions: What present did the Dauphin send Henry?
Why did Henry not wish for more soldiers before the battle?
How did the battle get its name?
answers: Tennis balls.
If they won, the glory was greater; if they died, England lost less.
From the nearby castle of Agincourt.

lessons.title: Chapter 54: Henry VI. of Windsor – The Story of the Maid of Orleans
steps: Read chapter 54 aloud together
Narrate how Joan of Arc led the French army and what happened to her
Find Domrémy, Orléans, Reims, and Rouen on a map of France
Add 'Joan of Arc relieves Orléans, 1429' and 'Hundred Years' War ends, 1453' to your timeline
questions: Why was Joan called the Maid of Orleans?
Where was the Dauphin crowned?
Why did the English say Joan was a witch?
answers: She drove the English away from Orleans.
At Rheims (Reims).
They thought no one else could have done such wonderful things.
lessons.notes: Joan was burned at Rouen in 1431; consider previewing that sentence. The book dates the war's end to 1451; most historians use 1453.

lessons.title: Chapter 55: Henry VI. of Windsor – The Red Rose and the White
steps: Read chapter 55 aloud together
Narrate how the red and white roses became badges and how Richard of York claimed the throne
Find St Albans in Hertfordshire and the city of York on a map of England
Add 'First Battle of St Albans; Wars of the Roses begin, 1455' to your timeline
questions: Which rose did the Yorkists wear, and which did the Lancastrians wear?
What did the Duke of York do in the House of Lords?
Whom did the London crowd choose as king at the end?
answers: York wore white; Lancaster wore red.
He sat on the throne and claimed it.
Edward, Duke of York (Edward IV).
lessons.notes: The rose-plucking scene comes from Shakespeare, not from records. The deaths of the Duke and his twelve-year-old son at Wakefield (1460) are told in some detail.

lessons.title: Chapter 56: Edward IV. – The Story of Queen Margaret and the Robbers
steps: Read chapter 56 aloud together
Narrate how Queen Margaret and her son escaped the robbers in the forest
Find Towton in Yorkshire and Hexham in Northumberland on a map
Add 'Battle of Towton, 1461' to your timeline
questions: What was the weather like at the battle of Towton?
How did Margaret get away from the first robbers?
What did the second robber do for the Queen and Prince?
answers: A wild storm of wind and snow.
She ran off with her son while they quarreled over her jewels.
He hid them in his cave, fed them, and took them to a ship.
lessons.notes: The robber story (often set after Hexham, 1464) is a traditional tale, not well documented.

lessons.title: Chapter 57: Edward IV. – The Story of the King-Maker
steps: Read chapter 57 aloud together
Narrate how Warwick the King-maker changed sides and what happened in the mist at Barnet
Find Barnet north of London and Tewkesbury in Gloucestershire on a map
Add 'Battles of Barnet and Tewkesbury, 1471' to your timeline
questions: Why was the Earl of Warwick called the King-maker?
Why did some Red Rose soldiers attack their own side at Barnet?
What badge did Edward's men wear on their coats?
answers: He was powerful enough to put Edward on the throne, and later Henry again.
In the mist they mistook the Earl of Oxford's star badge for Edward's sun.
A golden sun.
lessons.notes: Several killings are told plainly: Prince Edward stabbed, Henry VI's mysterious death, and Clarence drowned in wine (a tradition).

lessons.title: Chapter 58: Edward V. – The Story of the King Who Was Never Crowned
steps: Read chapter 58 aloud together
Narrate how Richard of Gloucester got both young princes and took the crown
Find Ludlow Castle in Shropshire and Westminster Abbey in London on a map
Add 'Edward V reigns but is never crowned, 1483' to your timeline
questions: Where did Queen Elizabeth take her younger son for safety?
Who persuaded her to give up little Richard?
What did the people do when Dr. Shaw called Richard their true king?
answers: Westminster Abbey, as sanctuary.
A bishop.
They stood silent and did not cheer.
lessons.notes: This picture of Richard III follows Tudor writers who were hostile to him; historians still debate his character. Lord Hastings' sudden execution is described.

lessons.title: Chapter 59: Richard III. – The Story of the Two Little Princes in the Tower
steps: Read chapter 59 aloud together
Narrate what happened to the princes in the Tower and how Richard III died at Bosworth
Find Bosworth Field near Market Bosworth in Leicestershire on a map
Add 'Princes in the Tower disappear, 1483' and 'Battle of Bosworth, 1485' to your timeline
questions: Who was the one servant left with the princes?
Where was Richard's crown found after the battle?
Which lord changed sides in the middle of the battle?
answers: Black Bill.
Under a hawthorn tree.
Lord Stanley.
lessons.notes: The smothering of the princes is told gently but clearly; preview for young children. What happened to them is still unproven. Richard's skeleton was found under a Leicester car park in 2012.

lessons.title: Chapter 60: Henry VII. – The Story of a Make-Believe Prince
steps: Read chapter 60 aloud together
Narrate who Lambert Simnel pretended to be and how Henry VII proved him false
Find Dublin in Ireland and Stoke (East Stoke) in Nottinghamshire on a map
Add 'Lambert Simnel defeated at the Battle of Stoke, 1487' to your timeline
questions: How did Henry VII bring the White and Red Roses together?
How did Henry show Londoners that Simnel was a fake?
What jobs did Henry give Lambert Simnel?
answers: He married Elizabeth of York, daughter of Edward IV.
He paraded the real Earl of Warwick through the streets.
Kitchen scullion, then keeper of the King's falcons.

lessons.title: Chapter 61: Henry VII. – The Story of Another Make-Believe Prince
steps: Read chapter 61 aloud together
Narrate Perkin Warbeck's adventures and how his rebellion ended
Find St Michael's Mount in Cornwall, Exeter, and Taunton on a map
Add 'Perkin Warbeck surrenders, 1497' and 'Columbus reaches America, 1492' to your timeline
questions: Whom did Perkin Warbeck claim to be?
What were the two great discoveries of this time?
Who brought printing to England?
answers: Richard, Duke of York, the younger prince from the Tower.
Printing and America.
Caxton.

lessons.title: Chapter 62: Henry VIII. – The Story of the Field of the Cloth of Gold
steps: Read chapter 62 aloud together
Narrate the splendors of the Field of the Cloth of Gold and what happened in the wrestling match
Find Guînes near Calais in northern France on a map
Add 'Field of the Cloth of Gold, 1520' to your timeline
questions: What was Wolsey's father's trade?
What happened to King Francis's grand tent?
Who won the wrestling match between the two kings?
answers: He was a butcher.
A strong wind snapped the ropes and blew it down.
King Francis.

lessons.title: Chapter 63: Henry VIII. – How the King Became the Defender of the Faith and How the Great Cardinal Died
steps: Read chapter 63 aloud together
Narrate how Henry won the title Defender of the Faith and why he later quarreled with the Pope
Find Wittenberg in Germany and Leicester in England on a map
Add 'Henry VIII named Defender of the Faith, 1521' and 'Wolsey dies at Leicester, 1530' to your timeline
questions: What does 'Fidei Defensor' mean, and where can you still see it?
Who began the Reformation in Germany?
Why did Henry turn against Wolsey?
answers: Defender of the Faith; as F.D. or Fid. Def. on British coins.
Martin Luther.
The Pope would not let Henry put away Katherine, and Anne Boleyn turned Henry against him.
lessons.notes: The book is written from a Protestant viewpoint; a short talk about how Catholics and Protestants each saw these events may help.

lessons.title: Chapter 64: Henry VIII. – The Story of the King's Six Wives
steps: Read chapter 64 aloud together
Narrate what happened to each of Henry VIII's six wives
Find Kleve (Cleves) in Germany, home of Anne of Cleves, on a map
Add 'Henry VIII breaks with Rome, 1534' and 'Henry VIII dies, 1547' to your timeline
questions: Why did Henry dislike Anne of Cleves when he met her?
Why were the church Bibles chained to desks?
What did the rebels of the Pilgrimage of Grace say was their leader?
answers: She looked nothing like her portrait and could speak no English.
Books were costly, so they were chained in case someone stole them.
Poverty.
lessons.notes: The chapter lists several beheadings, including two of Henry's wives. The rhyme 'divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived' can help children remember the wives.

lessons.title: Chapter 65: Edward VI. – The Story of a Boy King
steps: Read chapter 65 aloud together
Narrate why the poor were angry about enclosures and what Ket did under the Oak of Reformation
Find Norwich in Norfolk and Bodmin in Cornwall on a map
Add 'Edward VI becomes king, 1547' and 'Kett's Rebellion, 1549' to your timeline
questions: How did enclosing the common lands hurt poor people?
What did Ket call the great tree in his camp?
Whom did Edward VI name to be queen after him?
answers: They could no longer graze their cows and sheep there.
The Oak of Reformation.
His cousin, Lady Jane Grey.
lessons.notes: The tale of the Mayor of Bodmin being hanged on his own gallows is grim; parents may wish to preview it.

lessons.title: Chapter 66: The Story of Lady Jane Grey
steps: Read chapter 66 aloud together
Narrate how Lady Jane Grey was made queen against her wishes and how Mary took the crown
Find the Tower of London on a map of London and Spain on a map of Europe
Add 'Lady Jane Grey reigns nine days; Mary I becomes queen, 1553' to your timeline
questions: How did Lady Jane feel when she was offered the crown?
What did Jane say when her father told her the reign was over?
Why did the English dislike Mary's plan to marry Philip of Spain?
answers: Sad and frightened; she fainted.
That those were the happiest words she had heard since being made queen.
They feared Spain and its cruel Inquisition.
lessons.notes: Jane's beheading is told briefly. The nickname 'Bloody Mary' reflects a Protestant view; a short discussion of both sides can help.

lessons.title: Chapter 67: Mary I. – How the Princess Elizabeth Became a Prisoner
steps: Read chapter 67 aloud together
Narrate how Princess Elizabeth was taken to the Tower and the story of the little boy with flowers
Trace the River Thames to the Tower of London, then find Hatfield in Hertfordshire
Add 'Princess Elizabeth imprisoned in the Tower, 1554' to your timeline
questions: Why did Elizabeth refuse at first to land at the Traitors' Gate?
What did the little boy bring Elizabeth?
What did Elizabeth say she would rather be when she heard a milkmaid singing?
answers: She said she was no traitor.
Flowers.
A free milkmaid rather than a princess who was a prisoner.

lessons.title: Chapter 68: Mary I. – How a Candle Was Lit in England Which Has Never Been Put Out
steps: Read chapter 68 aloud together
Narrate what Latimer said to Ridley and what he meant by the candle
Find Oxford, where Latimer and Ridley died, and Calais on a map
Add 'Latimer and Ridley burned at Oxford, 1555' and 'Calais lost; Mary I dies, 1558' to your timeline
questions: What did Latimer say they would light in England?
Which town did England lose at the end of Mary's reign?
What did Mary say would be found on her heart?
answers: A candle that would never be put out.
Calais.
The word 'Calais'.
lessons.notes: The chapter speaks of burnings for religion (about 280 people), without graphic detail. It praises the Protestant martyrs; you might note that Catholics were also put to death for their faith under other rulers.

lessons.title: Chapter 69: Elizabeth – How the Imprisoned Princess Became a Queen
steps: Read chapter 69 aloud together
Narrate how Elizabeth heard she was queen and what she said entering the Tower
Find Hatfield House in Hertfordshire and the Tower of London on a map
Add 'Elizabeth I becomes queen, 17 November 1558' to your timeline
questions: Where was Elizabeth sitting when she heard she was queen?
How did Elizabeth enter the Tower this time compared with before?
What did the people love to call her?
answers: Under an oak tree at Hatfield.
As a free queen, not a prisoner through the Traitors' Gate.
Good Queen Bess.
lessons.notes: The book says no one was killed for religion under Elizabeth; in fact many Catholic priests and some others were executed during her reign.

lessons.title: Chapter 70: Elizabeth – The Story of a Most Unhappy Queen
steps: Read chapter 70 aloud together
Narrate how the Little Douglas helped Mary escape and what happened to her in England
Find Loch Leven in Scotland and Fotheringhay in Northamptonshire on a map
Add 'Mary, Queen of Scots escapes Loch Leven, 1568' and 'Mary executed, 1587' to your timeline
questions: How were Elizabeth and Mary, Queen of Scots related?
What did the Little Douglas do with the castle keys?
How many years was Mary kept a prisoner in England?
answers: They were cousins.
He dropped them in the loch.
Nineteen years.
lessons.notes: Mary's execution is described with some detail (the block, her little dog); consider previewing the end.

lessons.title: Chapter 71: Elizabeth – The Story of How England Was Saved from the Spaniards
steps: Read chapter 71 aloud together
Narrate Drake's game of bowls and how the Spanish Armada was beaten and scattered
Find Cádiz in Spain, Plymouth in Devon, and the Armada's route round Scotland and Ireland
Add 'Defeat of the Spanish Armada, 1588' to your timeline
questions: What did Drake call his raid on the Spanish harbor?
What was Drake doing when the Armada was sighted?
Why could the English ships fight better than the Spanish ones?
answers: Singeing the King of Spain's beard.
Playing bowls.
They were smaller and easier to turn, and the wind favored them.
lessons.notes: Drake's game of bowls is a much-loved legend that cannot be proven.

lessons.title: Chapter 72: Elizabeth – The Story of Sir Walter Raleigh
steps: Read chapter 72 aloud together
Narrate the story of Raleigh's cloak and the servant who threw water over him
Find Virginia and Roanoke Island on a map of the eastern United States
Add 'Raleigh sends colonists to Roanoke, Virginia, 1585' and 'Sir Philip Sidney dies, 1586' to your timeline
questions: How did Raleigh first win the Queen's notice?
Why did Raleigh name the new land Virginia?
What did Sir Philip Sidney do with his cup of water?
answers: He laid his new cloak over a puddle for her.
To honor Elizabeth, the 'Virgin Queen'.
Gave it to a dying soldier who needed it more.
lessons.notes: The cloak and water-bucket stories are legends. The book overstates Raleigh's role with tobacco and potatoes, which reached Europe through several people.

lessons.title: Chapter 73: Elizabeth – The Story of the Queen's Favorite
steps: Read chapter 73 aloud together
Narrate the quarrels of Elizabeth and Essex and the story of the lost ring
Find Ireland, where Essex was sent to govern, and the Tower of London on a map
Add 'Earl of Essex executed, 1601' and 'Elizabeth I dies, 24 March 1603' to your timeline
questions: Why did the Queen box Essex's ears?
What went wrong with the ring Essex sent?
Who became king after Elizabeth?
answers: He rudely turned his back on her.
The boy gave it to the wrong lady, who kept it hidden.
Her cousin James, King of Scotland.
lessons.notes: The ring story is a legend that appeared long after Essex's death.

units.title: Unit 9: The Stuarts and the Civil War (Chapters 74–82)

lessons.title: Chapter 74: James VI. of Scotland, I. of England – The Story of Guy Fawkes
steps: Read chapter 74 aloud together
Narrate how the Gunpowder Plot was planned and how Guy Fawkes was caught
Find the Houses of Parliament at Westminster in London and Edinburgh in Scotland on a map
Add 'James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England, 1603' and 'Gunpowder Plot, 5 November 1605' to your timeline
questions: How many barrels of gunpowder were hidden in the cellar?
How was the plot discovered?
How do people in Britain still remember the day?
answers: Thirty-six.
A warning letter sent to a Catholic lord was shown to the King.
With bonfires and fireworks on 5 November.
lessons.notes: Guy Fawkes' torture is mentioned briefly. The book notes Catholics were treated even more harshly afterward, a good point for discussion.

lessons.title: Chapter 75: James VI. of Scotland, I. of England – The Story of the "Mayflower"
steps: Read chapter 75 aloud together
Narrate why the Pilgrims left England and how they lived through their first winter
Find Plymouth in Devon, England, and Plymouth in Massachusetts on a map
Add 'Mayflower Pilgrims land at Plymouth, December 1620' to your timeline
questions: Why did the Pilgrim Fathers leave England?
What did they name their new town, and why?
How many Pilgrims went home when the Mayflower sailed back?
answers: To be free to worship God in the way they thought right.
Plymouth, after the English town they sailed from.
None.
lessons.notes: The book calls Native Americans 'wild Red Indians', which is dated and unfair; the Wampanoag people, including Squanto and Massasoit, helped the colony survive. A short discussion is worthwhile.

lessons.title: Chapter 76: Charles I. – How a Woman Struck a Blow for Freedom
steps: Read chapter 76 aloud together
Narrate what Jenny Geddes did in St Giles and how Scotland resisted the new Prayer Book
Find Edinburgh and St Giles' Cathedral on a map of Scotland
Add 'Jenny Geddes riot at St Giles, 23 July 1637' and 'National Covenant signed, 1638' to your timeline
questions: What did King James mean by 'The King can do no wrong'?
What did Jenny Geddes throw at the Dean?
What was the National Covenant?
answers: That whatever the king did was right and people must obey without question.
Her stool.
A paper signed by thousands of Scots promising to fight for freedom of religion.
lessons.notes: Jenny Geddes may be partly legendary, though the 1637 riot was real. The book uses anti-Catholic cries like 'popery'; a short talk on religious freedom for all fits the chapter's ending.

lessons.title: Chapter 77: Charles I. – The Story of How the King and the Parliament Quarreled and at Last Fought
steps: Read chapter 77 aloud together
Narrate how Charles tried to seize the five members and how Cornet Joyce showed his 'commission'
Find Westminster in London and Naseby in Northamptonshire on a map of England
Add 'Civil War begins, 1642' and 'Battle of Naseby, 1645' to your timeline
questions: What did King Charles say when he found the five members had gone?
Why were Cromwell's soldiers called Ironsides?
What did Cornet Joyce point to when the King asked for his commission?
answers: 'I see the birds are flown.'
Cromwell drilled them into strong, disciplined, splendid soldiers
His mounted soldiers behind him
lessons.notes: The book presents the Civil War largely from a Parliamentary/Protestant angle; you might ask children what each side was fighting for.

lessons.title: Chapter 78: Charles I. – The Story of How the King Was Brought to His Death
steps: Read chapter 78 aloud together
Narrate the King's trial in Westminster Hall and how he behaved before his judges
Find Carisbrooke Castle on the Isle of Wight and Whitehall in London on a map
Add 'Charles I executed, 30 January 1649' to your timeline
questions: Where did Charles flee when he escaped from the army?
What was Pride's Purge?
How many times did Charles refuse to plead at his trial?
answers: Carisbrooke Castle on the Isle of Wight
Colonel Pride's soldiers turned away members of Parliament who disagreed with the army
Three times
lessons.notes: The chapter ends with the King's beheading described briefly; preview if you have sensitive listeners.

lessons.title: Chapter 79: The Commonwealth – The Adventures of a Prince

His wife locked him in a room
His 'crowning mercy'

lessons.title: Chapter 80: The Commonwealth – The Lord Protector
steps: Read chapter 80 aloud together
Narrate how Cromwell broke up the Long Parliament and what he said about the mace
Find the North Sea between England and Holland (the Netherlands) on a map

'That bauble'

lessons.title: Chapter 81: Charles II. – How the King Came to His Own, and How Death Walked in the Streets of London
steps: Read chapter 81 aloud together
Narrate how Charles II came back to England, then describe London during the plague
Find Dover and London on a map of England, and the River Thames
Add 'Restoration of Charles II, 1660' and 'Great Plague of London, 1665' to your timeline

A red cross and 'The Lord have mercy on us'
He left money and food on a stone and called to them from a distance

lessons.title: Chapter 82: Charles II. – The Story of How London Was Burned
steps: Read chapter 82 aloud together
Narrate how the Great Fire started, spread, and was finally stopped
Find the Tower of London and the Monument on a map of London

How did people finally stop the fire?

'Have his body'; prisoners must be brought to trial, not kept in prison forever

units.title: Unit 10: The Later Stuarts and the Union (Chapters 83–89)

lessons.title: Chapter 83: James II. of England and VII. of Scotland – The Fiery Cross
steps: Read chapter 83 aloud together
Narrate how a Highland chief used the Fiery Cross to gather his clan
Find Edinburgh and the Highlands of Scotland on a map
Add 'James II becomes king; Argyle's rising fails, 1685' to your timeline
questions: How was the Fiery Cross passed from village to village?
Why did Argyle's army scatter?
Why couldn't Argyle fire his pistols when he was caught?
answers: Swift runners carried it from one village to the next
His captains were jealous and would not obey him
The powder got wet when he sprang into the river
lessons.notes: The book's portrayal of James II and Catholics is strongly Protestant-biased; the torture and executions mentioned are real but not detailed.

lessons.title: Chapter 84: James II. of England and VII. of Scotland – The Story of King Monmouth
steps: Read chapter 84 aloud together
Narrate Monmouth's rising: his welcome, the battle at Sedgemoor, and his capture
Find Taunton and Sedgemoor in Somerset on a map of England
Add 'Battle of Sedgemoor and the Bloody Assize, 1685' to your timeline
questions: What did Monmouth's followers call him?
Where was the last real battle on English ground fought?
What was the Bloody Assize?
answers: King Monmouth
Sedgemoor
Judge Jeffreys's cruel court journey punishing the rebels
lessons.notes: Mentions torture and mass executions after Sedgemoor; the details are brief but you may want to preview.

lessons.title: Chapter 85: James II. of England and VII. of Scotland – The Story of the Seven Bishops
steps: Read chapter 85 aloud together
Narrate why the seven bishops refused the King and how the people treated them
Find the Tower of London and Cornwall on a map of England
Add 'Trial of the Seven Bishops, 1688' to your timeline
questions: What paper did James order to be read in the churches?
Which bishop came from Cornwall?
How did people celebrate when the bishops were set free?
answers: The Declaration of Indulgence
Trelawney
Bells, bonfires, and seven candles in their windows

lessons.title: Chapter 86: James II. of England and VII. of Scotland – William the Deliverer
steps: Read chapter 86 aloud together
Narrate how William of Orange came to Britain and why it was called the Glorious Revolution
Find Torbay in Devon on a map of England, and Holland across the North Sea
Add 'William of Orange lands at Torbay, 5 November 1688' to your timeline
questions: What words were written on William's banner?
What was the 'Protestant East Wind'?
Who became King and Queen together after James fled?
answers: 'I will maintain the liberties of England and the Protestant religion'
The wind that finally blew William's fleet to Britain
William and Mary
lessons.notes: The book calls James a 'Popish tyrant'; its anti-Catholic tone reflects its time and is worth a brief comment.

lessons.title: Chapter 87: William III. and Mary II. – The Story of Brave Londonderry
steps: Read chapter 87 aloud together
Narrate the siege of Londonderry and how the ships broke the boom
Find Londonderry (Derry), the River Foyle, and the River Boyne in Ireland
Add 'Siege of Londonderry, 1689' and 'Battle of the Boyne, 1690' to your timeline
questions: Who stirred up the people of Londonderry with a rousing sermon?
What had the enemy built across the river?
Which battle ended James's hopes in Ireland?
answers: A clergyman called Walker
A boom (a bar) to stop ships
The Battle of the Boyne
lessons.notes: These events still carry strong feeling in Ireland today; the book tells them from the Protestant side.

lessons.title: Chapter 88: William III. and Mary II. – The Story of a Sad Day in a Highland Glen
steps: Read chapter 88 aloud together
Narrate why the Macdonald chief was late with his oath and what the Campbells did at Glencoe
Find Glencoe and Killiecrankie in the Scottish Highlands on a map
Add 'Massacre of Glencoe, 1692' and 'Death of William III, 1702' to your timeline
questions: Why was the Macdonald chief late to swear his oath?
How did the Campbells deceive the Macdonalds?
What illness did Queen Mary die of?
answers: He went to the wrong town first, in deep winter
They stayed as guests for nearly two weeks before attacking
Smallpox
lessons.notes: The Glencoe massacre is described with killing and families dying in the snow; preview for younger children.

lessons.title: Chapter 89: Anne – How the Union Jack Was Made
steps: Read chapter 89 aloud together
Narrate how the English and Scottish flags were combined to make the Union Jack
Find Gibraltar on a map of Spain, and Blenheim in Bavaria, Germany
Add 'Act of Union: Great Britain formed, 1707' to your timeline
questions: Which fortress did Britain keep after the Peace of Utrecht?
What two crosses were joined first in the flag?
Why is the flag called the Union 'Jack'?
answers: Gibraltar
St. George's cross and St. Andrew's cross
James VI signed his name 'Jacques', which sounds like Jack
lessons.notes: The 'Jacques' explanation for the name 'Jack' is a traditional story; historians aren't sure where the name came from. Drawing the three crosses is a good hands-on activity.

lessons.title: Chapter 90: George I. – The Story of the Earl of Mar's Hunting Party
steps: Read chapter 90 aloud together
Narrate the Earl of Mar's 'hunting party' and what happened at Sheriffmuir
Find Hanover in Germany, and Sheriffmuir near Dunblane in Scotland
Add 'George I becomes king, 1714' and 'The Fifteen Jacobite rising, 1715' to your timeline
questions: What language could George I not speak?
What fell from the Pretender's standard, worrying the Highlanders?
Who won at Sheriffmuir?
answers: English
The golden ball from the top of the staff
Nobody clearly; each side claimed victory

lessons.title: Chapter 91: George II. – The Story of Bonnie Prince Charlie
steps: Read chapter 91 aloud together
Narrate how Bonnie Prince Charlie won the Highlanders and beat Johnnie Cope
Find Edinburgh, Holyrood, and Prestonpans on a map of Scotland
Add 'Bonnie Prince Charlie lands; Battle of Prestonpans, 1745' to your timeline
questions: Why was Walpole called a 'peace minister'?
What did Charlie mean by 'I have thrown away the scabbard'?
How long did the battle of Prestonpans last?
answers: He tried to keep Britain out of wars so it could prosper
There was no turning back; he would win or die
About five minutes

lessons.title: Chapter 92: George II. – The Story of Flora Macdonald
steps: Read chapter 92 aloud together
Narrate how Flora Macdonald helped the Prince escape disguised as her maid 'Betty'
Find Derby, Culloden near Inverness, and the Isle of Skye on a map
Add 'Battle of Culloden, 1746' to your timeline
questions: How far south did Charlie's army march before turning back?
Where was the last Jacobite battle fought?
What disguise did Flora Macdonald bring for the Prince?
answers: Derby
Culloden, near Inverness
A woman's dress, as her maid Betty
lessons.notes: Culloden and its aftermath were very bloody; the book mentions it briefly. The Skye escape is real, though some details are romanticized.

lessons.title: Chapter 93: George II. – The Story of the Black Hole of Calcutta
steps: Read chapter 93 aloud together
Narrate who Robert Clive was and how he rose from clerk to general
Find Calcutta (Kolkata) and Plassey in Bengal on a map of India
Add 'Black Hole of Calcutta, 1756' and 'Battle of Plassey, 1757' to your timeline
questions: What was Clive's job before he became a soldier?
What company carried on Britain's trade with India?
What battle did Clive win against the Indian prince?
answers: A clerk for the East India Company
The East India Company
Plassey
lessons.notes: This chapter tells events strictly from a British-imperial view; historians think the Black Hole death toll was exaggerated. Consider discussing how Indians might see the British takeover of their land.

lessons.title: Chapter 94: George II. – The Story of How Canada Was Won
steps: Read chapter 94 aloud together
Narrate how Wolfe's men climbed the cliff to the Heights of Abraham
Find Quebec and the St. Lawrence River on a map of Canada
Add 'Wolfe takes Quebec, 1759' to your timeline
questions: What poem did Wolfe recite in the boat?
How did the soldiers reach the top of the cliff?
What did Montcalm say when told he was dying?
answers: Gray's 'Elegy in a Country Churchyard'
By a narrow, steep path, climbing quietly in the dark
He was glad he would not see Quebec surrender
lessons.notes: The book presents the British Empire's growth as a glory; French Canadians and Native peoples saw it differently.

lessons.title: Chapter 95: George III. – The Story of How America Was Lost
steps: Read chapter 95 aloud together
Narrate why the Americans refused the tax and what happened at the Boston Tea Party
Find Boston on a map of the United States
Add 'Boston Tea Party, 1773' and 'Declaration of Independence, 4 July 1776' to your timeline
questions: Why did the Americans say the taxes were unjust?
How did the young men dress for the Tea Party?
Who led the American army?
answers: They had no members in Parliament
As Native Americans, with painted faces and feathers
George Washington
lessons.notes: The book uses the dated term 'Red Indians' and says they had nearly died out; you may want to correct this and use 'Native Americans'. It tells the Revolution from the British side.

lessons.title: Chapter 96: George III. – A Story of the Spinning-Wheel
steps: Read chapter 96 aloud together
Narrate Richard Arkwright's story from penny barber to inventor of the spinning-frame
Find Lancashire and Derbyshire, the heart of the early cotton mills, on a map of England
Add 'Arkwright's water-powered spinning frame, 1769' to your timeline
questions: What was Arkwright's first trade?
Why did Arkwright's wife smash his models?
What did the two old women think made the noise of his machine?
answers: A barber
She thought they were making the family poor
Evil spirits

lessons.title: Chapter 97: George III. – England Expects That Every Man Will Do His Duty
steps: Read chapter 97 aloud together
Narrate Nelson's signal before Trafalgar and his last words aboard the Victory
Find Cape Trafalgar off the south coast of Spain on a map
Add 'Act of Union with Ireland, 1801' and 'Battle of Trafalgar, 21 October 1805' to your timeline
questions: What signal did Nelson send to the whole fleet?
What was the name of Nelson's ship?
Why did Nelson cover his face and medals when he was carried below?
answers: 'England expects that every man will do his duty'
The Victory
So his sailors would not see he was hurt and lose heart
lessons.notes: The book calls Napoleon an 'ogre'; children may enjoy hearing that the French saw him very differently.

lessons.title: Chapter 98: George III. – The Battle of Waterloo
steps: Read chapter 98 aloud together
Narrate the Battle of Waterloo and what Wellington meant by 'Night or Blücher'
Find Waterloo near Brussels in Belgium, the island of Elba, and St. Helena on a map
Add 'Battle of Waterloo, 18 June 1815' to your timeline
questions: Why was the Peninsular War given that name?
To which small island was Napoleon first sent?
Where was Napoleon sent after Waterloo?
answers: It was fought in Spain and Portugal, which form a peninsula
Elba
St. Helena, in the Atlantic Ocean

lessons.title: Chapter 99: George IV. – The First Gentleman in Europe
steps: Read chapter 99 aloud together
Narrate how George IV acted Irish, German, and Scottish on his visits, and what he refused
Find Dublin, Hanover, and Leith near Edinburgh on a map
Add 'Catholic Emancipation Act, 1829' to your timeline
questions: Why was George III called Farmer George?
Why was George IV called 'the first gentleman in Europe'?
What did the Catholic Emancipation Act allow?
answers: He loved peaceful country life
He was handsome with fine manners
Catholics could sit in Parliament and hold public posts

lessons.title: Chapter 100: William IV. – The Story of Two Peaceful Victories
steps: Read chapter 100 aloud together (see parent note first)
Narrate why the Reform Bill was needed and how slavery in the colonies was ended
Find the West Indies (Caribbean) and West Africa on a world map
Add 'Great Reform Act, 1832' and 'Slavery abolished in British colonies, 1834' to your timeline
questions: What was unfair about which places sent members to Parliament?
Who worked for many years to end slavery?
How much money did Parliament pay the planters?
answers: Empty places sent members while big factory towns sent none
Wilberforce (with Macaulay and others)
Twenty million pounds
lessons.notes: This chapter contains a racial slur, written to describe how slave-owners thought; consider rewording it when reading aloud. Note the planters, not the enslaved people, were compensated.

lessons.title: Chapter 101: Victoria – The Girl Queen
steps: Read chapter 101 aloud together
Narrate how young Victoria learned she would be Queen, and how she was woken with the news
Find Kensington Palace and Windsor Castle on a map of London and its surroundings
Add 'Victoria becomes Queen, 1837' to your timeline
